opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think partial credit is really valuable, and it's tied closely to some of the work we did on emergent abilities. The basic observation was that many of the "emergent" jumps people reported, where a model seems to suddenly acquire a capability at a certain scale, depend heavily on how you score the task.

Take arithmetic. Say you ask a model to multiply two multi-digit numbers and you use exact match: either every digit is right or you get zero. That's a very harsh, discontinuous metric. A model could be steadily improving, getting more digits right and making smaller mistakes, and exact match won't show any of it. Then once per-digit accuracy is high enough that the whole string comes out right, the score shoots up, and it looks like something qualitatively new appeared.

If you switch to something with partial credit, like token edit distance or per-digit accuracy, the picture often changes a lot. The improvement looks smooth and fairly predictable as you scale the model. So the "emergence" partly reflects the researcher's choice of metric rather than some sudden change inside the model.

That doesn't mean exact match is wrong. If you need a calculator, a number that's off by one digit is useless, so for deployment the all-or-nothing view may be exactly what matters. But for science, for understanding how capabilities develop and for forecasting what bigger models will do, partial credit gives you a much richer signal. It shows you the trend before the threshold.

So my view is that it's less about picking one right metric and more about being deliberate. Ask what question you're trying to answer. If it's "is this usable for my application," use the metric that matches your real requirements. If it's "how is this capability changing with scale or training," you want continuous, partial-credit measures. Otherwise you can end up surprised by things that were actually quite predictable.

r001.rationale: The response explains that partial-credit measures reveal steady improvements, such as more correct digits, before exact-match scores change.

r002.rationale: The response says apparent emergence depends heavily on scoring choice and that metric choice can change how scaling results look.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I've thought about a lot, because it gets at a deeper question of what we actually mean when we say a model is "good" at a task. Take arithmetic. If you ask a model to add two large numbers and it gets most of the digits right but one is off, the standard way we evaluate that is to say it's just wrong. Zero credit. Exact match or nothing. And there's a case for that, right? If I'm using this for my taxes, close doesn't count. But from the standpoint of understanding what the model has actually learned, that binary view throws away a tremendous amount of information.

So the argument for partial credit is really about measurement. If I score a model on, say, a distance metric, how far off was the answer, or how many digits were correct, I can see a smooth progression as models scale. I can see that a model is learning the carry operation, or that it's handling the first few digits reliably and falling apart at the end. That tells me something about the mechanism and where the failure is. Whereas with exact match, you often see what looks like a sharp jump, a so-called emergent capability, and some of our work has argued that a lot of that sharpness is an artifact of the metric. The underlying competence was improving gradually all along. The discontinuity lives in how we chose to score it.

Now, I want to be careful here, because partial credit can also mislead you. If I give a model 90 percent for getting nine out of ten digits, that number suggests a kind of reliability that doesn't exist for the end user. Nobody wants a calculator that's right 90 percent of the way. So I think the right framing is that these are answering different questions. Exact match is answering, can I deploy this? Partial credit is answering, what has this system learned, and how is it changing as I scale or train it? And a lot of the confusion in the field, honestly, comes from using one metric to answer the other question.

The other thing I'd say is that the choice of partial-credit metric is itself a modeling decision. Digit-level accuracy, numerical distance, log-probability of the correct answer, these all encode different assumptions about what "closer" means, and they'll give you different curves. So I don't think there's one right answer. What I push for is that people be explicit about which question they're asking, report more than one view when they can, and be really skeptical of dramatic claims that rest entirely on a single discontinuous metric.

r001.rationale: It says partial-credit metrics can show a smooth progression as models scale, revealing gradual learning that exact-match scores may hide.

r002.rationale: It states that different partial-credit metrics encode different assumptions and produce different curves, affecting how results and capability claims are interpreted.

astra-6.text:
I think partial credit is useful because getting the final answer wrong doesn’t tell you everything about what a model can do. In arithmetic, a model might follow the right procedure and make one calculation error, or it might fundamentally misunderstand the operation. If we score both as simply incorrect, we lose that distinction.

But the partial credit has to reflect something meaningful. A number being close to the correct answer doesn’t necessarily mean the model used a better procedure. So I’d want to look at which steps were valid and where the failure occurred, alongside whether the final answer was correct. That gives us a richer diagnostic picture, while still recognizing that, for some applications, you really do need the exact answer.

r001.rationale: The response says partial credit gives a richer diagnostic picture, but does not state that it captures gradual changes in model performance.

r002.rationale: It explains that scoring both kinds of wrong answers as simply incorrect loses a meaningful distinction, while partial credit can provide richer diagnostics—showing that the metric affects how results are interpreted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think partial credit can be useful, but it depends on what you’re trying to measure. If you ask a model an arithmetic question and it gets the answer wrong, exact-match accuracy tells you something important: it didn’t solve the problem. But it doesn’t tell you whether it made a small computational mistake or fundamentally misunderstood the task.

Partial credit can help distinguish those cases. The challenge is deciding what deserves credit. A number that’s close to the correct answer doesn’t necessarily reflect better reasoning, and a plausible-looking explanation may still be invalid. So I’d want to reward meaningful intermediate steps that we can actually verify.

I see those as complementary measurements. Did it get the answer right? And, separately, what can we learn about how it failed? That second question can be very useful for improving the model.

r001.rationale: The response says partial credit can distinguish types of errors and help diagnose failures, but it does not say it captures gradual changes in model performance.

r002.rationale: The response explains that exact-match accuracy and partial credit provide different information, depending on what is being measured, which communicates that metric choice affects how results are interpreted.
